entries.944566381294de58ed4894a4b83ec4d4bbba24cd: <div sID="gen19718" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Hos.3" sID="Hos.3"/> <div eID="gen19718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19719" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19720" type="x-p"/> God is still by the prophet inculcating the same thing upon this careless people, and much in the same manner as before, by a type or sign, that of the dealings of a husband with an adulterous wife. In this chapter we have, I. The bad character which the people of Israel now had; they were, as is said of the Athenians (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.16">Acts xvii. 16</reference>), "wholly given to idolatry," <reference osisRef="Hos.3.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The low condition which they should be reduced to by their captivity, and the other instances of God's controversy with them, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.2-Hos.3.4">ver. 2-4</reference>. III. The blessed reformation that should at length be wrought upon them in the latter days, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">ver. 5</reference>.
entries.78cc1709cd58315b6c230fdd25e7c507326db504: <div eID="gen19720" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19719" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Idolatry of Israel; The Prophet's Remonstrances; Promises to the Penitent. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  760.)</title> <div sID="gen19721" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then said the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto me, Go yet, love a woman beloved of <hi type="italic">her</hi> friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine. <hi type="super">2</hi> So I bought her to me for fifteen <hi type="italic">pieces</hi> of silver, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> a homer of barley, and a half homer of barley: <hi type="super">3</hi> And I said unto her, Thou shalt abide for me many days; thou shalt not play the harlot, and thou shalt not be for <hi type="italic">another</hi> man: so <hi type="italic">will</hi> I also <hi type="italic">be</hi> for thee. <hi type="super">4</hi> For the children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice, and without an image, and without an ephod, and <hi type="italic">without</hi> teraphim: <hi type="super">5</hi> Afterward shall the children of Israel return, and seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, and David their king; and shall fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> and his goodness in the latter days. <div eID="gen19721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19722" type="x-p"/> Some think that this chapter refers to Judah, the two tribes, as the adulteress the prophet married (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.3">ch. i. 3</reference>) represented the <hi type="italic">ten tribes;</hi> for this was not to be divorced, as the ten tribes were, but to be left desolate for a long time, and then to return, as the two tribes did. But these are called the <hi type="italic">children of Israel,</hi> which was the ten tribes, and therefore it is more probable that of them this parable, as well as that before, is to be understood. <hi type="italic">Go,</hi> and repeat it, says God to the prophet; <hi type="italic">Go yet again.</hi> Note, For the conviction and reduction of sinners it is necessary that precept be upon precept, and line upon line. If they will not believe one sign, try another, <reference osisRef="Exod.4.8-Exod.4.9">Exod. iv. 8, 9</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen19722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19723" type="x-p"/> I. In this parable we may observe, <div eID="gen19723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19724" type="x-p"/> 1. God's goodness and Israel's badness strangely serving for a foil to each other, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.1">v. 1</reference>. Israel is as a woman <hi type="italic">beloved of her friend,</hi> either of him that has married her or of him that only courts her, and <hi type="italic">yet an adulteress;</hi> such is the case between God and Israel. We say of those whose affection is mutual that there is <hi type="italic">no love lost</hi> between them; but here we find a great deal of the love even of God himself lost and thrown away upon an unworthy ungrateful people. The God of Israel retains a very great love for the <hi type="italic">children of Israel,</hi> and yet they are an evil and adulterous generation. <hi type="italic">Be astonished, O heavens! at this, and wonder, O earth!</hi> (1.) That God's goodness has not put an end to their badness; the Lord loves them, has a kindness for them, and is continually showing kindness to them; they know it, they cannot but own it, that he has been as a friend and Father to them; and yet they <hi type="italic">look to other gods,</hi> gods that they can see, and to the love of which they are drawn by the eye; they look to them with an eye of adoration (they offer up all their services to them) and with an eye of dependence (they expect all their comforts from them); if they were restrained from bowing the knee to idols, yet they gave them an amorous glance, and had <hi type="italic">eyes full of that</hi> spiritual <hi type="italic">adultery.</hi> And they loved <hi type="italic">flagons of wine;</hi> they joined with idolaters because they lived merrily and drank hard; they had a kindness for <hi type="italic">other gods</hi> for the sake of the plenty of good wine with which they had been sometimes treated in their temples. Idolatry and sensuality commonly go together; those that make a god of their belly, as drunkards do, will easily be brought to make a god of any thing else. God's priests were to <hi type="italic">drink no wine</hi> when they went in to minister, and his Nazarites none at all. But the worshippers of other gods <hi type="italic">drank wine in bowls;</hi> nay, no less than <hi type="italic">flagons of wine</hi> would content them. (2.) That their badness had not stopped the current of his favours to them. This is a wonder of mercy indeed, that she is thus <hi type="italic">beloved of her friend, though an adulteress;</hi> such is the <hi type="italic">love of the Lord towards the children of Israel.</hi> "Go," says God, "<hi type="italic">love</hi> such a woman; see if thou canst find in thy heart to do it. No, thou canst not, the breast of no man would admit such a love; yet such is my <hi type="italic">love to the children of Israel;</hi> it is love to the loveless, to the unlovely, to those that have a thousand times forfeited it." Note, In God's goodwill to poor sinners his thoughts and ways are infinitely above ours, and his love is more condescending and compassionate than ours is, or can be; in this, as much as any thing, he is <hi type="italic">God, and not man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.11.9">Hos. xi. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen19724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19725" type="x-p"/> 2. The method found for the bringing of a God so very good and a people so very bad together again; this is the thing aimed at, and what God aims at he will accomplish. To our great surprise, we find a breach thus wide as the sea effectually healed; miracles cease not so long as divine mercy does not cease. Observe here, (1.) The course God takes to humble them and make them know themselves (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and a homer and a half of barley,</hi> that is, I courted her to be reconciled, to leave her ill courses, and return to her first husband, as <reference osisRef="Hos.2.14">ch. ii. 14</reference>. I <hi type="italic">allured</hi> her, and <hi type="italic">spoke comfortably</hi> to her; as the <hi type="italic">Levite who went after</hi> his concubine that had <hi type="italic">played the harlot</hi> from him, and had run away with another man, <hi type="italic">spoke friendly to her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.19.3">Judg. xix. 3</reference>. But here the present which the prophet brought her for the purchasing of her favour is observed to be a very small one; but it was all that was intended for her separate maintenance, and in it she is reduced to a short allowance, and, to punish her for her pride, is made to look very mean. When Samson went to be reconciled to his wife that had disobliged him he <hi type="italic">visited her with a kid</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.15.1">Judg. xv. 1</reference>), which was a genteel entertainment. But the prophet here visited his wife with <hi type="italic">fifteen pieces of silver,</hi> a small sum, which yet she must be content to live upon a great while, so long as till her husband thought fit to restore her to her first estate. She shall also have <hi type="italic">a homer and a half of barley,</hi> for bread-corn, and that is all she must expect till she be sufficiently humbled, and, by a competent time of trial, satisfactory proof given that she is indeed reformed. Let her be made sensible that it is not for her own merit that her husband makes court to her; it is but a lame price that he values her at. The price of a servant was thirty shekels, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.32">Exod. xxi. 32</reference>. This was but half so much; yet let her know that it is more than she is worth. God had given Egypt for Israel's ransom once, so precious were they then in his sight, and so honourable, <reference osisRef="Isa.43.3">Isa. xliii. 3, 4</reference>. But now that they have gone a whoring from him he will give but fifteen pieces of silver for them, so much have they lost in their value by their iniquity. Note, Those whom God designs honour and comfort for he first makes sensible of their own worthlessness, and brings them to acknowledge, with the prodigal, <hi type="italic">I am no more worthy to be called thy son.</hi> Time was when Israel was <hi type="italic">fed with the finest of the wheat,</hi> but they grew wanton, <hi type="italic">and loved flagons of wine,</hi> and therefore, in order to the humbling and reducing of them, they must be brought in the land of their captivity to eat barley-bread, and be thankful they can get it, and to eat that too by weight and measure, whereas they did not use to be stinted. Note, Poverty and disgrace sometimes prove a happy means of making great sinners true penitents. (2.) The new terms upon which God is willing to come with them (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt abide for me many days, and shalt not be for another, so will I be for thee.</hi> He might justly have given them a bill of divorce, and have resolved to have no more to do with them; but he is willing to show them kindness, and that the matter should be compromised; he deals not with them in strict justice, according to the rigour of the law, but according to the multitude of his mercies; and it represents God's gracious dealings with the apostate race of mankind, that had gone a whoring from him; he bought them indeed with an inestimable price, not for their honour, but for the honour of his own justice; and now this is the proposal he makes to them, the covenant of grace he is willing to enter into with them—they must be to him a people, and he will be to them a God, the same with the proposal here made to Israel. [1.] They must take to themselves the shame of their apostasy from him, must submit to, and accept of, the punishment of their iniquity: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt abide for me many days</hi> in <hi type="italic">solitude</hi> and <hi type="italic">silence,</hi> as a widow that is <hi type="italic">desolate</hi> and in sorrow; they must <hi type="italic">lay aside their ornaments,</hi> and wait with patience and submission to know what God will do with them, and whether he will please to admit such unworthy wretches into his favour again, as they did <reference osisRef="Exod.33.4-Exod.33.5">Exod. xxxiii. 4, 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Their father,</hi> their husband, has <hi type="italic">spit in their face</hi> (as God said concerning Miriam), has put them under the marks of his displeasure, and therefore, like her, they must be <hi type="italic">ashamed seven days,</hi> and be <hi type="italic">shut out of the camp</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.12.14">Num. xii. 14</reference>), till <hi type="italic">their uncircumcised hearts be humbled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.41">Lev. xxvi. 41</reference>. Let them <hi type="italic">sit alone</hi> and <hi type="italic">keep silence, waiting for the salvation of the Lord,</hi> and in the mean time let them <hi type="italic">bear the yoke,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.26-Lam.3.28">Lam. iii. 26-28</reference>. Let them not expect that God should speedily return in mercy to them,; no, let them want it, let them wait for it <hi type="italic">many days,</hi> during all the days of their captivity, and reckon it a miracle of mercy, and well worth waiting for, it if come at last. Note, Those whom God designs mercy for he will first bring to abase themselves and to put a high value upon his favours. [2.] They must never return to folly again; that is the condition upon which God will <hi type="italic">speak peace to his people and to his saints</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">Ps. lxxxv. 8</reference>), and no other. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt not play the harlot,</hi> shalt not worship idols in the land of thy captivity, while thou art there set apart for the uncleanness." Note, It is not enough to take shame to ourselves for the sins we have committed, and to justify God in correcting us for them, but we must resolve, in the strength of God's grace, that we will not offend any more, that we will not again go a whoring from God, after the world and the flesh. Blessed be God, though it is the law of the covenant, it is not the condition of it that we shall never in any thing do amiss: "But thou shalt not <hi type="italic">play the harlot;</hi> thou shalt not serve other gods, <hi type="italic">shalt not be for another man.</hi>" In the land of their captivity they would be courted to worship the idols of the country; that would be a trial for them, a <hi type="italic">long</hi> trial, many days: "But if thou keep thy ground, and hold fast thy integrity, if, when <hi type="italic">all this comes upon thee,</hi> thou dost not <hi type="italic">stretch out thy hand to a strange god,</hi> thou wilt be qualified for the returns of God's favour." Note, It is a certain sign that our afflictions are means of much good to us, and earnests of more, when we are kept by the grace of God from being overcome by the temptations of an afflicted state. [3.] Upon these terms their Maker will again be their husband: <hi type="italic">So will I also be for thee.</hi> This is the covenant between God and returning sinners, that, if they will be for him to serve him, he will be for them to save them. Let them renounce and abjure all rivals with God for the throne in the heart, and devote themselves entirely to him and him only, and he will be to them a God all-sufficient. If we be faithful and constant to God in a way of duty, and will never leave nor forsake him, he will be so to us in a way of mercy, and will never leave nor forsake us. And a fairer proposal could not be made. <div eID="gen19725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19726" type="x-p"/> II. In the <reference osisRef="Hos.3.4-Hos.3.5">last two verses</reference> we have the interpretation of the parable and the application of it to Israel. <div eID="gen19726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19727" type="x-p"/> 1. They must long <hi type="italic">sit like a widow,</hi> stripped of all their joys and honours, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1-Lam.4.2">Lam. iv. 1, 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">They shall abide many days without a king, and without a prince;</hi> and a nation in this condition may well be called <hi type="italic">a widow.</hi> They want the blessing, (1.) Of civil government: They shall abide <hi type="italic">without a king,</hi> and <hi type="italic">without a prince,</hi> of their own. There were kings and princes over them to oppress them and rule them with rigour, but they had no king nor prince to protect them, to fight their battles for them, to administer justice to them, and to take care of their common safety and welfare. Note, Magistracy is a very great blessing to a people, and it is a sad and sore judgment to want it. (2.) Of public worship: <hi type="italic">They shall</hi> abide <hi type="italic">without a sacrifice,</hi> and <hi type="italic">without an image</hi> (or a <hi type="italic">statue,</hi> or <hi type="italic">pillar;</hi> the word is used concerning the pillars Jacob erected, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.18">Gen. xxviii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.31.45">xxxi. 45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.20">xxxv. 20</reference>), and <hi type="italic">without an ephod and teraphim.</hi> The <hi type="italic">teraphim</hi> being here closely joined to the <hi type="italic">ephod,</hi> some thing the <hi type="italic">urim</hi> and <hi type="italic">thummim</hi> were meant by it in the breast-plate of the high priest. The meaning is that in their captivity they should not only have no face of a nation upon them, but no face of a church; they should not have (as a learned expositor speaks) liberty of any public profession or exercise of religion, either true or false, according to their choice. They shall have <hi type="italic">no sacrifice or altar</hi> (so the LXX.), and therefore no sacrifice because no altar. They shall have <hi type="italic">no ephod,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">teraphim,</hi> no legal priesthood, no means of knowing God's mind, no oracle to consult in doubtful cases, but shall be all in the dark. Note, The case of those is very melancholy that are deprived of all opportunities to worship God in public. This was the case of the Jews in their captivity; and it is so far the case of the scattered Jews at this day that, though they have their synagogues, they have no temple-service. Desolate indeed is their condition that are shut out from communion with God, that have no opportunity of directing their addresses to God by sacrifice and altar, and of receiving instruction from him by ephod and teraphim. <div eID="gen19727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19728" type="x-p"/> 2. They shall at length be received again as a wife (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Afterwards,</hi> in process of time, when they have gone through this discipline, <hi type="italic">they shall return,</hi> that is, they shall repent of their idolatries and forsake them, they shall apply themselves to God and adhere to him, and herein they shall be accepted of him. Two things are here promised as instances of their return, and steps towards their acceptance with God in their return:—(1.) The enquiries they shall make after God: <hi type="italic">They shall seek the Lord their God, and David their king.</hi> Note, Those that would find God, and find favour with him, must seek him, must ask after him, covet acquaintance with him, desire to be reconciled to him, set their love on him, and labour in this that they may be accepted of him. Their seeking him implies that they had lost him, that they were lamenting their loss, and that they were solicitous to retrieve what they had lost. They shall seek him as <hi type="italic">their God;</hi> for <hi type="italic">should not a people seek unto their God?</hi> And they shall seek <hi type="italic">David their King,</hi> who can be no other than the Messiah, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of David, the <hi type="italic">root and offspring of David,</hi> whom David himself called <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>), and to whom God gave the <hi type="italic">throne of his father David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Luke i. 32</reference>. The Chaldee reads it, They shall <hi type="italic">seek the service of the Lord their God,</hi> and <hi type="italic">shall obey Messiah, the Son of David their king.</hi> Compare this with <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jer. xxx. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Ezek. xxxiv. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.25">xxxvii. 25</reference>. Note, Those that would seek the Lord so as to find him must apply to Jesus Christ, and must seek to him as their King, and become his willing people, and take an oath of fealty and allegiance to him. (2.) The reverence they shall have of God: <hi type="italic">They shall fear the Lord and his goodness.</hi> Some by his <hi type="italic">goodness</hi> here understand the temple, towards which they shall look, in worshipping God. The Jews say, There were three things which Israel cast off in the days of Rehoboam—the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven,</hi> the <hi type="italic">family of David,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">house of the sanctuary;</hi> and it will never be well with them till they return, and seek them all three, which is here promised. They shall seek the kingdom of heaven in <hi type="italic">the Lord their God,</hi> the royal family in <hi type="italic">David their King,</hi> and the temple in <hi type="italic">the goodness of the Lord.</hi> Others by <hi type="italic">his goodness</hi> understand Christ, the same <hi type="italic">with David their King.</hi> But it is rather to be taken for that attribute of God which he showed as his glory, and by which he proclaimed his name. Note, It is not only the Lord and his greatness that we are to fear, but the Lord and his goodness, not only his majesty, but his mercy. They shall <hi type="italic">flee for fear to the Lord and his goodness</hi> (so some take it), shall flee to it as their city of refuge. We must <hi type="italic">fear God's goodness,</hi> that is, we must admire it, and stand amazed at it, must adore it, and <hi type="italic">worship</hi> as Moses did at the proclaiming of this name, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Exod. xxxiv. 6</reference>. We must be afraid of offending his goodness, of making any ungrateful returns for it, and so forfeiting it. <hi type="italic">There is forgiveness with God, that he may be feared,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Ps. cxxx. 4</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">rejoice with trembling</hi> in the goodness of God, must not be <hi type="italic">high-minded, but fear.</hi> Now this promise had its accomplishment when by the gospel of Christ great multitudes both of Jews and Gentiles were brought home to God, and incorporated in the New-Testament church, served God in Christ, with a filial fear of divine grace, and were accepted of God as his Israel. And some think it is to be yet further accomplished in the conversion of those Jews to the faith of Christ who shall remain in unbelief, when they shall seek their Messiah as <hi type="italic">David their King,</hi> and by him <hi type="italic">all Israel shall be saved,</hi> when the <hi type="italic">fulness of the Gentiles is brought in.</hi> Time was when they sought him to put him to death, saying, <hi type="italic">We have no king but Cæsar;</hi> but the day is coming when they shall seek him to <hi type="italic">appoint him their head,</hi> and to lay their necks under his yoke. He that has here promised that they shall do it will enable them to do it, and bring about this great work in his own way and time, <hi type="italic">in the latter days</hi> of the <hi type="italic">last times,</hi> the times of the Messiah: but, alas! who shall live when God does this? How far we are to expect a general conversion of that nation I cannot say; but I am sure we ought to pray that the Jews may be converted.  <chapter eID="Hos.3"/> <div eID="gen19728" type="x-p"/>

entries.4d64246790fc5b11e9f07aa3201804c34c2fda28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12272"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.3.1-Hos.3.5">Ho 3:1-5</reference>. Israel's Condition in Their Present Dispersion, Subsequent to Their Return from Babylon, Symbolized.</title> <div sID="gen22344" type="x-p"/> The prophet is to take back his wife, though unfaithful, as foretold in <reference osisRef="Hos.1.2">Ho 1:2</reference>. He purchases her from her paramour, stipulating she should wait for a long period before she should be restored to her conjugal rights. So Israel is to live for a long period without her ancient rites of religion, and yet be free from idolatry; then at last she shall acknowledge Messiah, and know Jehovah's goodness restored to her.<div eID="gen22344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22345" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12272"/><hi type="bold">1. Go yet--</hi>"Go again," referring to <reference osisRef="Hos.1.2">Ho 1:2</reference> [Henderson].<div eID="gen22345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a woman--</hi>purposely indefinite, for thy wife, to express the separation in which Hosea had lived from Gomer for her unfaithfulness.<div eID="gen22346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beloved of her friend--</hi>used for "her husband," on account of the estrangement between them. She was still beloved of her husband, though an adulteress; just as God still loved Israel, though idolatrous (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.20">Jr 3:20</reference>). Hosea is told, not as in <reference osisRef="Hos.1.2">Ho 1:2</reference>, "take a wife," but "love" her, that is, renew thy conjugal kindness to her.<div eID="gen22347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who look to other gods--</hi>that is, have done so heretofore, but henceforth (from the return from Babylon) shall do so no more (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flagons of wine--</hi>rather, pressed cakes of dried grapes, such as were offered to idols (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">Jr 7:18</reference>) [Maurer]. <div eID="gen22349" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c54d225421ba1fa3d9a604ffcb6324dd4808736: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12273"/><div sID="gen22350" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12273"/><hi type="bold">2. I bought her--</hi>The price paid is too small to be a probable dowry wherewith to buy a wife from her parents; but it is just half the price of a female slave, in money, the rest of the price being made up in grain (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.32">Ex 21:32</reference>). Hosea pays this for the redemption of his wife, who has become the slave of her paramour. The price being half grain was because the latter was the allowance of food for the slave, and of the coarsest kind, not wheat, but barley. Israel, as committing sin, was the slave of sin (<reference osisRef="John.8.34">Joh 8:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.6.16-Rom.6.20">Ro 6:16-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.19">2Pe 2:19</reference>). The low price expresses Israel's worthlessness. <div eID="gen22350" type="x-p"/>
entries.75bd150f8b12154dcbcc3eb6a031bfa20393c8ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12274"/><div sID="gen22351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12274"/><hi type="bold">3. abide for me--</hi>separate from intercourse with any other man, and remaining for me who have redeemed thee (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.21.13">De 21:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so will I also be for thee--</hi>remain for thee, not taking any other consort. As Israel should long remain without serving other gods, yet separate from Jehovah; so Jehovah on His part, in this long period of estrangement, would form no marriage covenant with any other people (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>). He would not immediately receive her to marriage privileges, but would test her repentance and discipline her by the long probation; still the marriage covenant would hold good, she was to be kept separated for but a time, not divorced (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Is 50:1</reference>); in God's good time she shall be restored. <div eID="gen22352" type="x-p"/>
entries.f50fc0e3165ed4b3fb1ae06284134a1db0bfe092: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12275"/><div sID="gen22353" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12275"/>4. The long period here foretold was to be one in which Israel should have no civil polity, king, or prince, no sacrifice to Jehovah, and yet no idol, or false god, no ephod, or teraphim. Exactly describing their state for the last nineteen centuries, separate from idols, yet without any legal sacrifice to Jehovah, whom they profess to worship, and without being acknowledged by Him as His Church. So Kimchi, a Jew, explains it. The ephod was worn by the high priest above the tunic and robe. It consisted of two finely wrought pieces which hung down, the one in front over the breast, the other on the back, to the middle of the thigh; joined on the shoulders by golden clasps set in onyx stones with the names of the twelve tribes, and fastened round the waist by a girdle (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.6-Exod.28.12">Ex 28:6-12</reference>). The common ephod worn by the lower priests, Levites, and any person performing sacred rites, was of linen (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.14">2Sa 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.27">1Ch 15:27</reference>). In the breast were the Urim and Thummim by which God gave responses to the Hebrews. The latter was one of the five things which the second temple lacked, and which the first had. It, as representing the divinely constituted priesthood, is opposed to the idolatrous "teraphim," as "sacrifice" (to Jehovah) is to "an (idolatrous) image." "Abide" answers to "thou shalt abide for me" (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.3">Ho 3:3</reference>). Abide in solitary isolation, as a separated wife. The teraphim were tutelary household gods, in the shape of human busts, cut off at the waist (as the root of the Hebrew word implies) [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Ge 31:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.30-Gen.31.35">30-35</reference>). They were supposed to give responses to consulters (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.24">2Ki 23:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.21">Eze 21:21</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.2">Zec 10:2</reference>). Saul's daughter, Michal, putting one in a bed, as if it were David, proves the shape to have been that of a man. <div eID="gen22353" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e4e4cfdf339546036c8929075fbcc81aa900310: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12276"/><div sID="gen22354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12276"/><hi type="bold">5. Afterward--</hi>after the long period ("many days," <reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>) has elapsed.<div eID="gen22354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return--</hi>from their idols to "their God," from whom they had wandered.<div eID="gen22355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">David their king--</hi>Israel had forsaken the worship of Jehovah at the same time that they forsook their allegiance to David's line. Their repentance towards God is therefore to be accompanied by their return to the latter. So Judah and Israel shall be one, and under "one head," as is also foretold (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Ho 1:11</reference>). That representative and antitype of David is Messiah. "David" means "the beloved." Compare as to Messiah, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>. Messiah is called David (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jr 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.24">37:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen22356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fear the Lord and his goodness--</hi>that is, tremblingly flee to the Lord, to escape from the wrath to come; and to His goodness," as manifested in Messiah, which attracts them to Him (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.12">Jr 31:12</reference>). The "fear" is not that which "hath torment" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.18">1Jo 4:18</reference>), but reverence inspired by His goodness realized in the soul (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the latter days--</hi>those of Messiah [Kimchi]. <chapter eID="Hos.3"/>

entries.a3b23dba658ad3209d9653037aa7d003eb92f9c3: <div eID="gen33594" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33595" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33596" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33596" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33595" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33597" type="x-p"/> By the prophet's taking back his wife, for whom he (her friend or husband) still retained has affection, though she had proved unfaithful; by his entering into a new contract with her; and by his giving her hopes of reconciliation, after she should for some time prove, as in a state of widowhood, the sincerity of her repentance; is represented the gracious manner in which God will restore the Jews from the Babylonish captivity, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.1-Hos.3.4">Hos 3:1-4</reference>. It is also very strongly intimated that the whole house of Israel will be added to the Church of Christ in the latter days, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos 3:5</reference>. <div eID="gen33597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33598" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33599" type="x-p"/> Go ye, love a woman - This is a different command from that mentioned in the first chapter. That denoted the infidelity of the kingdom of Israel, and God's divorce of them. He gave them up to their enemies, and caused them to be carried into captivity. The woman mentioned here represents one who was a lawful wife joining herself to a paramour; then divorced by her husband; afterwards repenting, and desirous to be joined to her spouse; ceasing from her adulterous commerce, but not yet reconciled to him. This was the state and disposition of the Jews under the Babylonish captivity. Though separated from their own idols, they continued separated from their God. He is still represented as having affectionate feelings towards them; awaiting their full repentance and contrition, in order to renew the marriage covenant. These things are pointed out by the symbolical actions of the prophet. <div eID="gen33599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33600" type="x-p"/> Beloved of her friend - Or, a lover of evil; or, loving another: for the Hebrew words אהבת רע mean one who loves evil or a friend: because רע signifies a friend, or evil, according as it is pointed. The former seems to be its best sense here; רע rea is a friend; רע ra is evil. <div eID="gen33600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33601" type="x-p"/> According to the love of the Lord - This woman, who had proved false to her husband, was still beloved by him, though he could not acknowledge her; as the Israelites were beloved by the Lord, while they were looking after other gods. The flagons of wine were probably such as were used for libations, or drunk in idol feasts. Others think that the words should be translated cakes of dried grapes, sweet cakes, consecrated wafers.
entries.d064b26cad28f24cb0f57af91654d7569f276e6d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33602" type="x-p"/> Fifteen pieces of silver - If they were shekels, the price of this woman was about two pounds five shillings. <div eID="gen33602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33603" type="x-p"/> A homer of barley - As the homer was about eight bushels, or something more, the homer and half was about twelve or thirteen bushels.
entries.7dc2078479a7372e6e3b093fc156feae7652ead1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33604" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt abide for me many days - He did not take her home, but made a contract with her that, if she would abstain from her evil ways, he would take her to himself after a sufficient trial. In the meantime he gave her the money and the barley to subsist upon, that she might not be under the temptation of becoming again unfaithful. <div eID="gen33604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33605" type="x-p"/> So will I also be for thee - That is, if thou, Israel, wilt keep thyself separate from thy idolatry, and give me proof, by thy total abstinence from idols, that thou wilt be my faithful worshipper, I will receive thee again, and in the meantime support thee with the necessaries of life while thou art in the land of thy captivity. This is farther illustrated in the following verses.
entries.365845f738dae7599819e8e405a102fbc25090f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33606" type="x-p"/> Many days without a king - Hitherto this prophecy has been literally fulfilled. Since the destruction of the temple by the Romans they have neither had king nor prince, nor any civil government of their own, but have lived in different nations of the earth as mere exiles. They have neither priests nor sacrifices nor urim nor thummim; no prophet, no oracle, no communication of any kind from God. <div eID="gen33606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33607" type="x-p"/> Without an image ephod - teraphim - The Septuagint read, Ουδε ουσης θυσιας, ουδε οντος θυσιαστηριου, ουδε ἱερατειας, ουδε δηλων: "Without a sacrifice, without an altar, without a priesthood, and without oracles;" that is, the urim and thummim. The Vulgate, Arabic, and Syriac read nearly the same. Instead of מצבה matstsebah, an image, they have evidently read מזבח mizbeach, an altar; the letters of these words being very similar, and easily mistaken for each other. But instead of either, one, if not two, of Kennicott's MSS. has מנחה minchah, an oblation. <div eID="gen33607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33608" type="x-p"/> What is called image may signify any kind of pillar, such as God forbade them to erect <reference osisRef="Lev.26.1">Lev 26:1</reference>, lest it should be an incitement to idolatry. <div eID="gen33608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33609" type="x-p"/> The ephod was the high priest's garment of ceremony; the teraphim were some kind of amulets, telesms, or idolatrous images; the urim and thummim belonged to the breastplate, which was attached to the ephod. <div eID="gen33609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33610" type="x-p"/> Instead of teraphim some would read seraphim, changing the ת tau into ש sin; these are an order of the celestial hierarchy. In short, all the time that the Israelites were in captivity in Babylon, they seem to have been as wholly without forms of idolatrous worship as they were without the worship of God; and this may be what the prophet designs: they were totally without any kind of public worship, whether true or false. As well without images and teraphim, as they were without sacrifice and ephod, though still idolaters in their hearts. They were in a state of the most miserable darkness, which was to continue many days; and it has continued now nearly eighteen hundred years, and must continue yet longer, till they acknowledge him as their Savior whom they crucified as a blasphemer.
entries.135c016613e63b914b4cfcdf5e4e469f81b6acfe: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33611" type="x-p"/> Afterward shall the children of Israel return - Shall repent of their iniquities, and seek the Lord; lay aside their mock worship, and serve the true God in spirit and in truth. <div eID="gen33611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33612" type="x-p"/> And David their king - Or as the Targum, "They shall obey the Messiah, the Son of David their King;" and thus look believingly upon him whom they have pierced, and mourn. And then shall their long spiritual darkness and dismal captivity have an end; but not before. The Messiah, as David, is promised in <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jer 30:9</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Eze.24.23">Eze 24:23</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Eze.37.22-Eze.37.25">Eze 37:22-25</reference> (note), and in this place of Hosea. Some think that the family of David is intended; but if we go to the rigour of the letter, the house of Israel was scarcely ever perfectly submissive to David. And we know that after the death of Solomon they never acknowledged the house of David till they were all carried away captive; and certainly never since. And to say that Zerubbabel is here meant, is not supportable, as the very short and imperfect obedience of the Jews to Zerubbabel can never comport with the high terms of this and similar prophecies. We are obliged, therefore, from the evidence of these prophecies, from the evidence of the above facts, from the evidence of the rabbins themselves, and from the evidence of the New Testament, to consider these texts as applying solely to Jesus Christ, the promised Messiah, who has been a light to lighten the Gentiles, and will yet be the glory of his people Israel. There is a strange propensity in some men to deny these evidences of Christianity, while they profess to believe its doctrines.  <chapter eID="Hos.3"/> <div eID="gen33612" type="x-p"/>

entries.935f316b9e0f8037f89fb0fb402de6012dcd3a1e: <div eID="gen16189" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Adulteress and Her Fresh Marriage - Hos 3:1-5</title> <div sID="gen16190" type="x-p"/> “The significant pair are introduced again, but with a fresh application.” In a second symbolical marriage, the prophet sets forth the faithful, but for that very reason chastising and reforming, love of the Lord to rebellious and adulterous Israel. By the command of God he takes a wife, who lives in continued adultery, notwithstanding his faithful love, and places her in a position in which she is obliged to renounce her lovers, that he may thus lead her to return. Hos 3:1-3 contain the symbolical action; Hos 3:4, Hos 3:5 the explanation, with an announcement of the reformation which this proceeding is intended to effect. <div eID="gen16190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16191" type="x-p"/> Hos 3:1 <hi type="italic">“And Jehovah said to me, Go again, and love a woman beloved of her companion, and committing adultery, as Jehovah loveth the children of Israel, and they turn to other gods, and love raisin-cakes.” </hi> The purely symbolical character of this divine command is evident from the nature of the command itself, but more especially from the peculiar epithet applied to the wife. עוד is not to be connected with ויּאמר, in opposition to the accents, but belongs to לך, and is placed first for the sake of emphasis. Loving the woman, as the carrying out of the divine command in Hos 3:2 clearly shows, is in fact equivalent to taking a wife; and <hi type="italic">'âhabh</hi> is chosen instead of <hi type="italic">lâqach</hi>, simply for the purpose of indicating at the very outset the nature of the union enjoined upon the prophet. The woman is characterized as beloved of her companion (friend), and committing adultery. רע denotes a friend or companion, with whom one cherishes intercourse and fellowship, never a fellow-creature generally, but simply the fellow-creature with whom one lives in the closest intimacy (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.17-Exod.20.18">Exo 20:17-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.22.25">Exo 22:25</reference>, etc.). The רע (companion) of a woman, who loves her, can only be her husband or paramour. The word is undoubtedly used in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">Jer 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.20">Jer 3:20</reference>, and Sol 5:16, with reference to a husband, but never of a fornicator or adulterous paramour. And the second epithet employed here, viz., “committing adultery,” which forms an unmistakeable antithesis to אהבת רע, requires that it should be understood in this instance as signifying a husband; for a woman only becomes an adulteress when she is unfaithful to her loving husband, and goes with other men, but not when she gives up her beloved paramour to live with her husband only. If the epithets referred to the love shown by a paramour, by which the woman had annulled the marriage, this would necessarily have been expressed by the perfect or pluperfect. By the participles אהבת and מנאפת, the love of the companion and the adultery of the wife are supposed to be continued and contemporaneous with the love which the prophet is to manifest towards the woman. This overthrows the assertion made by Kurtz, that we have before us a woman who was already married at the time when the prophet was commanded to love her, as at variance with the grammatical construction, and changing the participle into the pluperfect. For, during the time that the prophet loved the wife he had taken, the רע who displayed his love to her could only be her husband, i.e., the prophet himself, towards whom she stood in the closest intimacy, founded upon love, i.e., in the relation of marriage. The correctness of this view, that the רע is the prophet as husband, is put beyond all possibility of doubt by the explanation of the divine command which follows. As Jehovah lovers the sons of Israel, although or whilst they turn to other gods, i.e., break their marriage with Jehovah; so is the prophet to love the woman who commits adultery, or will commit adultery, notwithstanding his love, since the adultery could only take place when the prophet had shown to the woman the love commanded, i.e., had connected himself with her by marriage. The peculiar epithet applied to the woman can only be explained from the fact intended to be set forth by the symbolical act itself, and, as we have already shown at p. 22, is irreconcilable with the assumption that the command of God refers to a marriage to be really and outwardly consummated. The words כּאהבת יי recal <reference osisRef="Deut.7.8">Deu 7:8</reference>, and והם פּנים וגו Deu 31:18. The last clause, “and loving grape-cakes,” does not apply to the idols, who would be thereby represented either as lovers of grape-cakes, or as those to whom grape-cakes were offered (Hitzig), but is a continuation of פּנים, indicating the reason why Israel turned to other gods. Grape or raisin cakes (on <hi type="italic">'ăshı̄shâh</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.19">2Sa 6:19</reference>) are delicacies, figuratively representing that idolatrous worship which appeals to the senses, and gratifies the carnal impulses and desires. Compare <reference osisRef="Job.20.12">Job 20:12</reference>, where sin is figuratively described as food which is sweet as new honey in the mouth, but turns into the gall of asps in the belly. Loving grape-cakes is equivalent to indulging in sensuality. Because Israel loves this, it turns to other gods. “The solemn and strict religion of Jehovah is plain but wholesome food; whereas idolatry is relaxing food, which is only sought after by epicures and men of depraved tastes” (Hengstenberg).
entries.b111c30f2040ff0b149f1df7ad43a78b7b1748ea: Hos 3:2 <hi type="italic">“And I acquired her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver, and a homer of barley, and a lethech of barley.” </hi>אכּרה, with <hi type="italic">dagesh lene</hi> or <hi type="italic">dirimens</hi> (Ewald, §28, b), from <hi type="italic">kârâh</hi>, to dig, to procure by digging, then generally to acquire (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.2.6">Deu 2:6</reference>), or obtain by trading (<reference osisRef="Job.6.27">Job 6:27</reference>; 40:30). Fifteen <hi type="italic">keseph</hi> are fifteen shekels of silver; the word <hi type="italic">shekel</hi> being frequently omitted in statements as to amount (compare Ges. §120, 4, Anm. 2). According to <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.11">Eze 45:11</reference>, the <hi type="italic">homer</hi> contained ten baths or ephahs, and a <hi type="italic">lethech</hi> (ἡμίκορος, lxx) was a half homer. Consequently the prophet gave fifteen shekels of silver and fifteen ephahs of barley; and it is a very natural supposition, especially if we refer to 2Ki 7:1; 2Ki 16:18, that at that time an ephah of barley was worth a shekel, in which case the whole price would just amount to the sum for which, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.21.32">Exo 21:32</reference>, it was possible to purchase a slave, and was paid half in money and half in barley. The reason for the latter it is impossible to determine with certainty. The price generally, for which the prophet obtained the wife, was probably intended to indicate the servile condition out of which Jehovah purchased Israel to be His people; and the circumstance that the prophet gave no more for the wife than the amount at which a slave could be obtained, according to Ecc. 21:32 and Zec 11:12, and that this amount was not even paid in money, but half of it in barley - a kind of food so generally despised throughout antiquity (<hi type="italic">vile hordeum</hi>; see at Num 5:15) - was intended to depict still more strikingly the deeply depressed condition of the woman. The price paid, moreover, is not to be regarded as purchase money, for which the wife was obtained from her parents; for it cannot be shown that the custom of purchasing a bride from her parents had any existence among the Israelites (see my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäologie</hi>, ii. §109, 1). It was rather the marriage present (<hi type="italic">mōhar</hi>), which a bridegroom gave, not to the parents, but to the bride herself, as soon as her consent had been obtained. If, therefore, the woman was satisfied with fifteen shekels and fifteen ephahs of barley, she must have been in a state of very deep distress.
entries.e765eecc5653ef71f865da11f119184b4e9074b6: Hos 3:3 <hi type="italic">“And I said to her, Many days wilt thou sit for me: and not act the harlot, and not belong to a man; and thus will I also towards thee.” </hi> Instead of granting the full conjugal fellowship of a wife to the woman whom he had acquired for himself, the prophet puts her into a state of detention, in which she was debarred from intercourse with any man. Sitting is equivalent to remaining quiet, and לי indicates that this is for the husband’s sake, and that he imposes it upon her out of affection to her, to reform her and grain her up as a faithful wife. היה לאישׁ, to be or become a man’s, signifies conjugal or sexual connection with him. Commentators differ in opinion as to whether the prophet himself is included or not. In all probability he is not included, as his conduct towards the woman is simply indicated in the last clause. The distinction between זנה and היה לאישׁ, is that the former signifies intercourse with different paramours, the latter conjugal intercourse; here adulterous intercourse with a single man. The last words, “and I also to thee” (towards thee), cannot have any other meaning, than that the prophet would act in the same way towards the wife as the wife towards every other man, i.e., would have no conjugal intercourse with her. The other explanations that have been given of these words, in which <hi type="italic">vegam</hi> is rendered “and yet,” or “and then,” are arbitrary. The parallel is not drawn between the prophet and the wife, but between the prophet and the other man; in other words, he does not promise that during the period of the wife’s detention he will not conclude a marriage with any other woman, but declares that he will have no more conjugal intercourse with her than any other man. This thought is required by the explanation of the figure in Hos 3:4. For, according to the former interpretation, the idea expressed would be this, that the Lord waited with patience and long-suffering for the reformation of His former nation, and would not plunge it into despair by adopting another nation in its place. But there is no hint whatever at any such though as this in Hos 3:4, Hos 3:5; and all that is expressed is, that He will not only cut off all intercourse on the part of His people with idols, but will also suspend, for a very long time, His own relation to Israel.
entries.ce369df0169994cd06670e2a9272d3c37082df23: Hos 3:4 <hi type="italic">“For the sons of Israel will sit for many days without a king, and without a prince, and without slain-offering, and without monument, and without ephod and teraphim.” </hi> The explanation of the figure is introduced with כּי, because it contains the ground of the symbolical action. The objects, which are to be taken away from the Israelites, form three pairs, although only the last two are formally connected together by the omission of אין before תּרפים, so as to form one pair, whilst the rest are simply arranged one after another by the repetition of אין before every one. As king and prince go together, so also do slain-offering and memorial. King and prince are the upholders of civil government; whilst slain-offering and memorial represent the nation’s worship and religion. מצּבה, monument, is connected with idolatrous worship. The “monuments” were consecrated to Baal (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.24">Exo 23:24</reference>), and the erection of them was for that reason prohibited even in the law (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.1">Lev 26:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.22">Deu 16:22</reference> : see at 1Ki 14:23); but they were widely spread in the kingdom of Israel (2Ki 3:2; 2Ki 10:26-28; 2Ki 17:10), and they were also erected in Judah under idolatrous kings (1Ki 14:23; 2Ki 18:4; 2Ki 23:14; <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.2">2Ch 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.1">2Ch 31:1</reference>). The <hi type="italic">ephod</hi> and <hi type="italic">teraphim</hi> did indeed form part of the apparatus of worship, but they are also specially mentioned as media employed in searching into the future. The <hi type="italic">ephod</hi>, the shoulder-dress of the high priest, to which the Urim and Thummim were attached, was the medium through which Jehovah communicated His revelations to the people, and was used for the purpose of asking the will of God (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9">1Sa 23:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.7">1Sa 30:7</reference>); and for the same purpose it was imitated in an idolatrous manner (Jdg 17:5; Jdg 18:5). The <hi type="italic">teraphim</hi> were Penates, which were worshipped as the givers of earthly prosperity, and also as oracular deities who revealed future events (see my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäol.</hi> §90). The prophet mentions objects connected with both the worship of Jehovah and that of idols, because they were both mixed together in Israel, and for the purpose of showing to the people that the Lord would take away both the Jehovah-worship and also the worship of idols, along with the independent civil government. With the removal of the monarchy (see at Hos 1:4), or the dissolution of the kingdom, not only was the Jehovah-worship abolished, but an end was also put to the idolatry of the nation, since the people discovered the worthlessness of the idols from the fact that, when the judgment burst upon them, they could grant no deliverance; and notwithstanding the circumstance that, when carried into exile, they were transported into the midst of the idolaters, the distress and misery into which they were then plunged filled them with abhorrence of idolatry (see at Hos 2:7). <div eID="gen16191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16192" type="x-p"/> This threat was fulfilled in the history of the ten tribes, when they were carried away with the Assyrian captivity, in which they continue for the most part to the present day without a monarchy, without Jehovah-worship, and without a priesthood. For it is evident that by Israel the ten tribes are intended, not only from the close connection between this prophecy and Hos 1:1-11, where Israel is expressly distinguished from Judah (Hos 1:7), but also from the prospect held out in Hos 3:5, that the sons of Israel will return to David their king, which clearly points to the falling away of the ten tribes from the house of David. At the same time, as the carrying away of Judah also is presupposed in Hos 1:7, Hos 1:11, and therefore what is said of Israel is transferred <hi type="italic">implicite</hi> to Judah, we must not restrict the threat contained in this verse to the Israel of the ten tribes alone, but must also understand it as referring to the Babylonian and Roman exile of the Jews, just as in the time of king Asa (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.2-2Chr.15.4">2Ch 15:2-4</reference>). The prophet Azariah predicted this to the kingdom of Judah in a manner which furnishes an unmistakeably support to Hosea’s prophecy.
entries.92adb0200d380037afdddab8b535ca2c32055b99: Hos 3:5 <hi type="italic">“Afterward will the sons of Israel turn and seek Jehovah their God, and David their king, and will go trembling to Jehovah and to His goodness at the end of the days.” </hi> This section, like the previous one, closes with the announcement of the eventual conversation of Israel, which was not indicated in the symbolical action which precedes it, but is added to complete the interpretation of the symbol. Seeking Jehovah their God is connected with seeking David their king. For just as the falling away of the ten tribes from the royal house of David was merely the sequel and effect of their inward apostasy from Jehovah, and was openly declared in the setting up of the golden calves; the true return to the Lord cannot take place without a return to David their king, since God has promised the kingdom to David and his seed for ever (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.13">2Sa 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:16</reference>), and therefore David is the only true king of Israel (<hi type="italic">their</hi> king). This King David, however, is no other than the Messiah. For although David received the promise of the everlasting continuance of his government, not with reference to his own person, but for his seed, i.e., his family; and on the ground of this promise, the whole of the royal house of David is frequently embraced under the expression “King David,” so that we might imagine that David is introduced here, not as an individual, but as signifying the Davidic family; yet we must not understand it on this account as referring to such historical representatives of the Davidic government as Zerubbabel, and other earthly representatives of the house of David, since the return of the Israelites to “their King David” was not to take place till <hi type="italic">'achârı̄th hayyâmı̄m</hi> (the end of the days). For “the end of the days” does not denote the future generally, but always the closing future of the kingdom of God, commencing with the coming of the Messiah (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.49.1">Gen 49:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Isa 2:2</reference>). <hi type="italic">Pâchad 'el Yehovâh</hi>, to shake or tremble to Jehovah, is a pregnant expression for “to turn to Jehovah with trembling;” i.e., either trembling at the holiness of God, in the consciousness of their own sinfulness and unworthiness, or else with anguish and distress, in the consciousness of their utter helplessness. It is used here in the latter sense, as the two parallels, Hos 5:15. “in their affliction they will seek me,” and Hos 11:11, “they shall tremble as a bird,” etc., clearly show. This is also required by the following expression, ואל־טוּבו, which is to be understood, according to Hos 2:7, as denoting the goodness of God manifested in His gifts. Affliction will drive them to seek the Lord, ad His goodness which is inseparable from Himself (Hengstenberg). Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.31.12">Jer 31:12</reference>, where “the goodness of the Lord” is explained as corn, new wine, oil, lambs, and oxen, these being the gifts that come from the goodness of the Lord (Zec 9:17; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>). He who has the Lord for his God will want no good thing.  <chapter eID="Hos.3"/> <div eID="gen16192" type="x-p"/>
